notes: The opening poem has partial alphabetic features, but the transmitted lines do not form an unbroken acrostic. The draft does not reconstruct missing lines. “Her place” in verse 8 most naturally looks toward Nineveh, though the name is not repeated there.
The thorn and drunkenness wording is difficult. The address shifts between the enemy and afflicted Judah; feminine and masculine Hebrew forms help distinguish them. The plotter is not named.
vocabulary: A prophetic pronouncement, here concerning Nineveh.
News of release from the oppressor, expressed through the arriving messenger’s feet.

notes: Verse 2 has “like Israel’s splendor,” not simply “and.” The fiery-metal and cypress terms in verse 3 are uncertain descriptions of military equipment. The protective screen in verse 5 may be siege equipment; the shifts between attacking and defending forces are compressed.

The river gates and dissolving palace do not provide a complete historical mechanism of the fall. Verse 7 may begin “it is decreed” or an otherwise uncertain name, Huzzab. Verse 8’s time phrase and verse 13’s “her/your” shift are retained rather than silently normalized.
vocabulary: Three similar-sounding Hebrew words pile up the city’s ruin.
The predatory household images lead directly to the judgment on the city’s chariots, prey, and messengers.
